gloss.light: Producers feed on light. The light level in the pool varies depending on the era and brightest inside tide bands, most of all at the height of the season.
gloss.era: Every 10–18 minutes the climate turns: the baseline light and the water’s temperature change, one tide wave is replaced, and the currents shift. In about one era in six the water stands low and the highest ground shows as islands of dry land. Each era is named for what marks it as it begins.
gloss.maps: One map over the view at a time. Light colors every point by the light a photosynthesizing cell would get there; Heat is a thermal camera, deep blue to teal to amber to white over a span from 2° below the background water to 10° above it, with a contour line every 2°; Tide shows the light the Tide brings and where its bands are heading. Its key (G, E, H) or gauge opens it, and again closes it.
gloss.haze: Warm water bends light like the air over a hot road. Off, the view holds still over warm water (boiling water still roils). Auto draws it, and Adaptation may turn it off while frames run late (what Auto holds now is underlined).
gloss.optimum: The temperature a species works best at (0-45°). It drifts by mutation, so lineages can follow the climate or find a warm or cold refuge. A spark of life creates a species suited to the water it sparked in.
gloss.torpor: Far below its optimum temperature (more than 1.25 tolerances) a cell goes torpid: it doesn't feed, swim, or divide. Torpid cells pay a quarter of their upkeep, dim in color, stop pulsing, and falls silent, until the water warms again.
gloss.heatwave: An deviation of the climate: for a few minutes the water background temperature rises (a heat wave) or falls (a cold snap) by 5–8°.
gloss.cyst: A dormant cell. An animal cell running out of energy with nothing to eat in reach may go dormant. It stops swimming, pulsing, turns gray, only leaking a little energy, and wakes at random, after about 45 seconds on average. Nothing can eat a cyst. Cysts are the seed bank that carries a lineage through hard times.
gloss.satiety: A hunter attacks animals less as they get more full. Once a hunter holds more energy than it needs to divide, it rests instead of killing.
gloss.stone: Sand, and the skeletons of calcifying cells. Stone never drifts and the living cannot pass through it. Attacks made from among stone sometimes miss, so prey shelters in reefs, and calcifying cells settle on their own reef while everything else must go around it. Sand in the pool at the start of a world lasts nearly an hour. A loose grain of reef stone crumbles within minutes and a tightly packed one lasts far longer, but a reef that spreads to fill most of the wider around it wears away fast. So reefs stay as separate patches.
gloss.adapting: The simulation may reduce render quality if it is unable to maintain full quality at a smooth frame rate. This describes the reason: frames running late, the GPU busy for nearly the whole frame, the device under pressure (hot or busy, where the browser reports it), or the browser’s own pace (it hands out frames more slowly than the screen refreshes while the page has little to do: only the frame rate is lowered then). With Target fps on Auto it lowers the frame rate to 30 first, then eases what Adaptation may (work done less often, effects, the render scale), and below 30 only once nothing else is left. Adaptation will gradually restore quality if conditions improve, returning to 60 fps last.
gloss.mind-flee: Flight: an animal that is not a hunter swims away from hunters near it. It swims harder the closer they get up to its swimming ability.
gloss.density: The most device pixels drawn per CSS pixel. High-density (Retina) screens look sharper at 2× but cost up to four times the pixels of 1×. Auto draws at 1× (up to 1.5× while filming). 1x is recommended for most devices.
gloss.targetfps: Frames per second that the system is aiming for, as a whole number of the screen’s refreshes so frames stay evenly spaced. 30 FPS halves the GPU’s work and saves battery; Display follows the screen’s refresh rate (120 on many phones and Macs), which costs the most. Simulated time keeps pace with real time at any rate. Auto aims for 60 and, when the device can’t keep up, drops to 30 before easing anything else, and lower (20 or 15) only once nothing else is left (shown beside Auto); it returns to 60 last, once everything else is back. A rate chosen is held even then.
guide.ecology.p1: Producers are photosynthetic cells, anchored colonies and free-floating drifters alike. Consumers are grazers that crop them, scavengers of husks and dung, and predators. Every world founds each of these niches at least twice. Several pressures shape which forms thrive:
guide.ecology.currents: Anchored producers thrive where currents run strong; drifting ones where they are calm. Bonded bodies live cheaply and resist attack but disperse poorly.
